claim: The rat hippocampus expresses representations related to past experiences during sharp-wave ripple (SWR) events.
source: The rat hippocampus expresses these types of representations during sharp-wave ripple (SWR) events
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established finding in the field.

claim: Previous work identified a minority of SWRs that contain 'replay' of spatial trajectories at approximately 20x the movement speed of the animal.
source: previous work identified a minority of SWRs that contain 'replay' of spatial trajectories at ∼20x the movement speed of the animal
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and references previous findings in the field, specifically citing work by Nádasdy et al., 1999; Lee and Wilson, 2002; Davidson et al., 2009; Karlsson and Frank, 2009 in the introduction.

claim: The large majority of replay events contain spatially coherent, interpretable content.
source: we find that the large majority of replay events contain spatially coherent, interpretable content
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data showing 86% of all SWRs contain spatially coherent content.

claim: Many replay events progress at real-world, rather than accelerated, movement speeds, consistent with actual experiences.
source: many events progress at real-world, rather than accelerated, movement speeds, consistent with actual experiences
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data showing stationary-continuous mixtures are the most common category.

claim: Rapid plasticity during an experience in the hippocampus is thought to drive the initial encoding of representations of events.
source: where rapid plasticity during an experience is thought to drive the initial encoding of representations of events (Eichenbaum and Cohen, 2004)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Eichenbaum and Cohen, 2004.

claim: Hippocampal replay during slow-wave sleep and periods of immobility during waking is thought to contribute to longer term storage and updating of event memories in distributed hippocampal-neocortical circuits.
source: hippocampal 'replay' of stored representations during both slow-wave sleep and periods of immobility during waking is thought to contribute to the longer term storage and updating of event memories in distributed hippocampal-neocortical circuits (Frankland and Bontempi, 2005; Carr et al., 2011; Joo and Frank, 2018)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Frankland and Bontempi, 2005; Carr et al., 2011; Joo and Frank, 2018.

claim: Hippocampal cells preferentially fire at specific locations in an environment in rodents.
source: hippocampal cells preferentially fire at specific locations in an environment
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about hippocampal place cells.

claim: Ensembles of hippocampal cells fire in sequence as the animal moves through a series of locations.
source: ensembles of cells fire in sequence as the animal moves through a series of locations
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about hippocampal sequential firing.

claim: Hippocampal cells can be reactivated during a sharp-wave ripple (SWR) event when the animal is asleep or immobile.
source: When the animal is asleep or immobile, hippocampal cells can be reactivated during a 'sharp-wave ripple' (SWR) event.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about SWR events.

claim: A subset of SWRs contain sequential firing similar to that seen during a previous experience.
source: A subset of SWRs contain sequential firing similar to that seen during a previous experience
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about replay.

claim: Sequential firing events during SWRs proceed at an average speed of approximately 10 meters per second, about 20x faster than the animal's usual movement speed.
source: previous work has reported that these sequential firing events proceed at an average speed of ∼10 meters per second, about 20x faster than the animal's usual movement speed (Nádasdy et al., 1999; Lee and Wilson, 2002; Davidson et al., 2009; Karlsson and Frank, 2009)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Nádasdy et al., 1999; Lee and Wilson, 2002; Davidson et al., 2009; Karlsson and Frank, 2009.

claim: Only a minority (approximately 5-45%) of hippocampal SWRs contain statistically identifiable, sequential replay.
source: the current consensus is that only a minority (∼5–45%) of hippocampal SWRs contain statistically identifiable, sequential replay (Davidson et al., 2009; Michon et al., 2019; Shin et al., 2019; Kaefer et al., 2020; Tingley and Peyrache, 2020b)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Davidson et al., 2009; Michon et al., 2019; Shin et al., 2019; Kaefer et al., 2020; Tingley and Peyrache, 2020b.

claim: Some SWRs contain spiking of neurons associated with single locations where animals are immobile.
source: some SWRs contain spiking of neurons associated with single locations where animals are immobile (Yu et al., 2017)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Yu et al., 2017.

claim: Two reports suggested that events representing a single location are only seen in young animals.
source: although two reports suggested that events that represent a single location are only seen in young animals (Farooq and Dragoi, 2019; Muessig et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Farooq and Dragoi, 2019; Muessig et al., 2019.

claim: The state space model uses a combination of movement dynamics of different speeds to capture the spatial content and time evolution of replay during SWRs.
source: we develop a state space model that uses a combination of movement dynamics of different speeds to capture the spatial content and time evolution of replay during SWRs
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a description of the method developed in this study.

claim: The state space model characterizes spatial representations during SWRs as a mixture of three underlying patterns of movement dynamics: stationary trajectories, continuous trajectories, and spatially fragmented trajectories.
source: Our model goes beyond previous approaches (Deng et al., 2016; Maboudi et al., 2018) by characterizing the spatial representations during SWRs as a mixture of three underlying patterns of movement dynamics: stationary trajectories, continuous trajectories that can progress at many times the typical speed of the animal, and spatially fragmented trajectories.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a description of the model developed in this study.

claim: The model uses clusterless decoding, which relates multiunit spike waveform features to position without spike sorting.
source: We show how this model can take advantage of clusterless decoding—which relates multiunit spike waveform features to position without spike sorting—giving us more information about the population spiking activity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a description of the method used in this study.

claim: The model was applied to spiking data during SWR events from 10 rats.
source: We apply this model to spiking data during SWR events from 10 rats
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a description of the data analyzed in this study.

claim: 96% of classified SWRs and 86% of all SWRs include spatially coherent structure.
source: We find that 96% (22,170 of 23,071) of classified SWRs and 86% (22,170 of 25,844) of all SWRs include spatially coherent structure
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data analysis.

claim: Only 14% of classified SWRs include any times with spatially incoherent structure.
source: We find that only 14% (3295 of 23,071) of classified SWRs include any times with spatially incoherent structure
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data analysis.

claim: 19% of classified SWRs included time periods where the decoded position was classified as continuous.
source: in our datasets, 4449 of 23,071 or 19% of classified SWRs included time periods where the decoded position was classified as continuous
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data analysis.

claim: 89% of SWRs contain at least one of the three dynamics or dynamic mixtures using a 0.80 threshold.
source: Using a 0.80 threshold, 89% (23,071 of 25,844) of SWRs contain at least one of the three dynamics or dynamic mixtures.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data analysis.

claim: The most common category of classified SWRs were those with only stationary-continuous mixtures (42% of classified SWRs).
source: the most common category of classified SWRs were those with only stationary-continuous mixtures (8944 of 21,433 or 42% of classified SWRs
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Stationary-continuous mixture events contain representations that move at slower speeds similar to those speeds experienced by the animal in the environment.
source: These events contain representations that move at slower speeds (Figure 5D)—similar to those speeds experienced by the animal in the environment (Figure 5G, median 17 cm/s for run periods and 4 cm/s for all times)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5G.

claim: The second most prevalent classification was exclusively stationary events (23% of classified SWRs).
source: The second most prevalent classification was exclusively stationary events (4858 of 21,433 or 23% classified SWRs
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data analysis.

claim: Approximately 7% of classified SWRs contained non-local stationary events (stationary events representing positions at least 30 cm from the animal).
source: We set a threshold of 30 cm distance from the animal to identify non-local stationary events and found such content in ∼7% of classified SWRs (1437 of 21,433 classified SWRs).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data analysis.

claim: Non-local stationary events most commonly represented reward wells or choice points.
source: These non-local stationary events most commonly represented reward wells or choice points (Figure 5E)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Spatially coherent events have smaller HPD regions than events with fragmented dynamics.
source: We find that spatially coherent events indeed have smaller HPD regions than events with fragmented dynamics.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data analysis.

claim: The average HPD region for spatially coherent dynamics was much smaller than spatially incoherent dynamics (median 24 cm vs. median 238 cm, p=2.2e-16).
source: For the spatially coherent dynamics, the average HPD region for each SWR was much smaller than the spatially incoherent dynamics (median 24 cm, spatially coherent vs. median 238 cm, spatially incoherent, p=2.2e-16, one-sided Mann-Whitney-U).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Most SWRs (70% of classified SWRs) were classified as having only a single dynamic or dynamic mixture.
source: We first note that most of the SWRs (14,989 of 21,433 or 70% of classified SWRs) were classified as having only a single dynamic or dynamic mixture
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The average median difference between actual and decoded location during movement is 7 cm (5-9 cm 95% CI).
source: We found that the average median difference between actual and decoded location is small (7 cm median difference, 5–9 cm 95% CI, for all times where the animal was moving greater than 4 cm/s, five-fold cross validation).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by cross-validation analysis.

claim: The model successfully captures the dynamics of the population spiking activity in the simulated example.
source: An examination of the two summaries shown in Figure 1E reveals that that the model successfully captures the dynamics of the population spiking activity in Figure 1A.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the simulated data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The model is relatively insensitive to the choice of probability of staying in a dynamic for a large range of plausible probabilities (between 0.96 and 0.993).
source: We found that for a large range of plausible probabilities of staying in one of the dynamics (between 0.96 and 0.993, corresponding to an expected duration between 25 and 150 ms), the model identified the movement dynamics consistently, with high probability
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Clusterless decoding provides a longer spatial extent of the event and a narrower estimate of the posterior probability of latent position compared to sorted spike decoding.
source: As predicted, the spatial extent of the event is longer and the estimate of the posterior probability of latent position is narrower for the clusterless model.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by comparison of Figure 2B,D vs Figure 2A,C.

claim: The clusterless model's access to a larger pool of data provides more information about the extent of the event and more certainty in the latent position and the dynamic.
source: This reflects the clusterless model's access to a larger pool of data that provides more information about the extent of the event and more certainty in the latent position and the dynamic
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an explanation for the differences between clusterless and sorted spike decoding.

claim: Ten male Long Evans rats (500-700 g, 4-9 months old) were trained on a W-track spatial alternation task.
source: Ten male Long Evans rats (500–700 g, 4–9 months old) were trained on a W-track spatial alternation task.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the experimental subjects.

claim: Neural activity was recorded in CA1, CA2, CA3, MEC, Subiculum, and DG depending on the rat.
source: Neural activity was recorded in CA1, CA2, CA3, MEC, Subiculum, and DG depending on the rat.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the recording locations.

claim: Only tetrodes located in the CA1, CA2, and CA3 subregions were used in this study.
source: We only used tetrodes located in the CA1, CA2, and CA3 subregions in this study.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing which data was included in the analysis.

claim: The model uses 2 ms time bins for decoding.
source: In our case, since replay has been shown to move at speeds much faster than the animal's speed (Davidson et al., 2009; Pfeiffer and Foster, 2015), we set the variance of the Gaussian to 6.0 cm. This ensures that with a 2 ms time step, the latent position is 95% likely to be within 4.90 cm of the previous latent position
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the model parameters.

claim: The probability of staying in a dynamic is set to 0.98 for each 2 ms time step, which corresponds to an expected duration of 100 ms.
source: Accordingly, we set the probability of staying in a dynamic to 0.98 for each 2 ms time step, which corresponds to an expected duration of 100 ms for staying in a particular dynamic
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the model parameters.

claim: The model uses acausal decoding, meaning it uses all information from both past and future spikes.
source: We use acausal decoding, meaning that we use all information from both past and future spikes, to estimate the joint posterior probability of position and dynamic
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the decoding approach.

claim: SWRs were detected using a permissive threshold to ensure inclusion of both rare large-amplitude events and much more common small-amplitude events.
source: We detected SWRs using a permissive threshold (see Materials and methods) to ensure that we include both the rare large-amplitude events as well as the much more common small-amplitude events.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the SWR detection method.

claim: Candidate SWR times were found by z-scoring the population power trace and finding times when the z-score exceeded two standard deviations for a minimum of 15 ms and the speed of the animal was less than 4 cm/s.
source: Candidate SWR times were found by z-scoring the population power trace of an entire recording session and finding times when the z-score exceeded two standard deviations for a minimum of 15 ms and the speed of the animal was less than 4 cm/s.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the SWR detection method.

claim: Only SWRs with spikes from at least two tetrodes were analyzed.
source: We only analyzed SWRs with spikes from at least two tetrodes.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the inclusion criteria for SWRs.

claim: The five classification categories are: stationary, continuous, fragmented, stationary-continuous-mixture, and fragmented-continuous-mixture.
source: Time periods during sharp wave ripples are labeled as stationary, continuous, or fragmented when the probability of each individual state is above 0.80, regardless of duration. Time periods are labeled as stationary-continuous-mixture or fragmented-continuous-mixture when the sum of stationary and continuous or fragmented and continuous are above 0.80, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the classification categories.

claim: Position shuffling by resampling with replacement resulted in only 9% of SWRs being classified, significantly less than the 89% seen for real data.
source: Only 9% of the SWRs are classified in the shuffled datasets, a value that is significantly less than that seen for the real data (p=0.02 for recording session 1, p=0.02 for recording session 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by shuffle analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Shuffling that preserves local correlations but reduces global spatial structure resulted in less spatially coherent and more spatially incoherent content compared to real data.
source: Using this shuffle, we found that there was still less spatially coherent and more spatially incoherent content compared to the real data (recording session #1, spatially coherent: 99% vs. 71%, p=0.02, real vs. shuffled; spatially incoherent: 22% vs. 61%, p=0.02, real vs. shuffled; recording session #2, spatially coherent: 95% vs. 63%, p=0.02, real vs. shuffled; spatially incoherent: 16% vs. 79%, p=0.02, real vs. shuffled; Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by shuffle analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: With a higher classification threshold of 0.95, 74% of all SWRs were classified and 99% of classified SWRs included spatially coherent content.
source: We find that, while this change slightly reduced the total fraction of classified SWRs (19,478 of 26,159 or 74% of all SWRs), an even higher fraction of the classified SWRs (19,317 of 19,478 or 99% classified SWRs) included spatially coherent content.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data analysis with a different threshold.

claim: Stationary-continuous mixture events frequently represent locations that were some distance away from the animal (mean trajectory distance 52 cm).
source: Nonetheless, both the slow-moving events and continuous events frequently represent locations that were some distance away from the animal (mean trajectory distance from animal's position: stationary-continuous-mixture 52 cm vs. continuous 43 cm, Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Continuous events frequently represent locations that were some distance away from the animal (mean trajectory distance 43 cm).
source: Nonetheless, both the slow-moving events and continuous events frequently represent locations that were some distance away from the animal (mean trajectory distance from animal's position: stationary-continuous-mixture 52 cm vs. continuous 43 cm, Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Stationary-continuous mixture events have a median duration of 73 ms.
source: These events contain representations that move at slower speeds (Figure 5D)—similar to those speeds experienced by the animal in the environment (Figure 5G, median 17 cm/s for run periods and 4 cm/s for all times)—and are sustained, but slightly shorter, on average, than events with continuous dynamics (median duration: stationary-continuous-mixture 73 ms vs. continuous 94 ms, Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Continuous events have a median duration of 94 ms.
source: These events contain representations that move at slower speeds (Figure 5D)—similar to those speeds experienced by the animal in the environment (Figure 5G, median 17 cm/s for run periods and 4 cm/s for all times)—and are sustained, but slightly shorter, on average, than events with continuous dynamics (median duration: stationary-continuous-mixture 73 ms vs. continuous 94 ms, Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: 47% of SWRs with stationary dynamics were entirely stationary for the entire duration of the SWR.
source: The second most prevalent classification was exclusively stationary events (4858 of 21,433 or 23% classified SWRs; 47% of SWRs with stationary dynamics were entirely stationary for the entire duration of the SWR).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data analysis.

claim: 46% of non-local stationary events (664 of 1437) were stationary throughout the duration of the SWR.
source: Of these, 46% (664 of 1437 stationary SWRs) were stationary throughout the duration of the SWR.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data analysis.

claim: Multiunit spiking rates were similar across the different dynamics.
source: We first calculated the multiunit spiking rates and found that these were similar across the different dynamics (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: All dynamics, including stationary and stationary-continuous mixtures, were driven by comparable levels of sustained spiking information.
source: This indicates that all dynamics, including stationary and stationary-continuous mixtures, were driven by comparable levels of sustained spiking information and could not be explained by the absence of spiking.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the multiunit spiking rate analysis.

claim: When using periods of high multiunit activity instead of SWRs to identify events, a larger proportion of stationary and stationary-continuous dynamics relative to continuous dynamics was still found.
source: Further corroborating this, we found that when we re-ran our analysis using periods of high multiunit activity instead of SWRs to identify events, we still found a larger proportion of stationary and stationary-continuous dynamics relative to the continuous dynamics (Figure 5—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3F.

claim: Results were robust to increasing the tetrode participation threshold from two up to five tetrodes active during the SWR.
source: First, we increased our tetrode participation threshold from two up to five tetrodes active during the SWR, to eliminate the possibility that events with a single tetrode with a high rate interneuron might drive the classification of stationary or stationary-continuous mixture dynamics during SWRs. We found that our results were robust to this increase in threshold (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Removing spikes with spike widths less than 0.3 ms had little effect on the proportion of SWRs with stationary and stationary-continuous mixture dynamics.
source: Next, we removed spikes that had spike widths of less than 0.3 ms to reduce the potential contribution of narrow-waveform inhibitory interneurons (Fox and Ranck, 1975). Similarly, this had little effect: we still observed a high proportion of SWRs with stationary and stationary-continuous mixture dynamics (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: When excluding putative interneurons based on spike width and firing rate using clustered data, many stationary and stationary-continuous mixtures in SWRs were still observed.
source: Using clustered data, we can more robustly categorize units as putative interneurons; thus, we then repeated this analysis on clustered data for 9 of the 10 animals, excluding putative interneurons based on spike width and firing rate and requiring that at least three putative pyramidal cells be active during the SWR. Although there were many fewer events to examine, we still observed many stationary and stationary-continuous mixtures in SWRs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Stationary and stationary-continuous mixtures tended to have narrow posteriors as characterized by 95% HPD region size.
source: Instead, we found that stationary and stationary-continuous mixtures tended to have narrow posteriors (as characterized by 95% HPD region size in Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The majority of events occur when the animal is moving at speeds less than 2 cm/s.
source: In addition, the majority of our events occur when the animal is moving at speeds less than 2 cm/s, as expected for SWRs (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: When restricting analyses to SWRs where the animal was moving at speeds less than 1 cm/s, similar proportions of SWRs with stationary and stationary-continuous mixture dynamics were found.
source: Further, when we restrict the analyses to SWRs where the animal was moving at speeds less than 1 cm/s, we find similar proportion of SWRs with stationary and stationary-continuous mixture dynamics (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Most SWRs contained spikes from multiple tetrodes, including those with stationary dynamics.
source: First, as mentioned above, most of our SWRs contained spikes from multiple tetrodes, including those with stationary dynamics (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Stationary dynamics have a median duration of 54 ms (38-74 ms quartiles).
source: Second, the stationary dynamics have a longer duration than one would expect from a burst alone (Figure 5B, 54 ms median duration, 38–74 ms quartiles vs. bursts which have a typical duration of 6–24 ms; Ranck Jr, 1973; Harris et al., 2001; Tropp Sneider et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5B and citations to Ranck Jr, 1973; Harris et al., 2001; Tropp Sneider et al., 2006.

claim: Only approximately 50% of the spikes had interspike intervals (ISIs) of less than 6 ms during the stationary, stationary-continuous, and continuous dynamics.
source: Third, only ∼50% of the spikes had interspike intervals (ISIs) of less than 6 ms during the stationary, stationary-continuous, and continuous dynamics (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: When using only CA1 tetrodes to decode, similar proportions of dynamics were obtained as when using all tetrodes.
source: However, we verified that when we used only CA1 tetrodes to decode (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E), we get similar proportions of dynamics as when using all the tetrodes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Approximately 12% of the classified events were identified as significant by the Radon method.
source: We found that ∼12% of the classified events (as defined by our state-space decoder) were identified as significant by this Radon method.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section comparing the state space model to standard approaches.

claim: Of the SWRs that contained a period of continuous dynamics, 31% (1386 of 4511 SWRs) were significant by the Radon method.
source: Of the SWRs that contained a period of continuous dynamics, 31% (1386 of 4511 SWRs) were significant.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section comparing the state space model to standard approaches.

claim: Of all SWRs that contained a period of stationary dynamics, 8% (542 of 7176 SWRs) were significant by the Radon method.
source: Of all SWRs that contained a period of stationary dynamics, 8% (542 of 7176 SWRs) were significant
evidence: This is stated in the Results section comparing the state space model to standard approaches.

claim: When restricted to long stationary events (>100 ms duration), 28% were significant by the Radon method.
source: and when we restricted the analysis to long stationary events (>100 ms duration), we found that 28% were significant.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section comparing the state space model to standard approaches.

claim: The linear regression method, which samples from the posterior probability and uses linear regression to fit a line, detects only non-zero slopes as significant and thus cannot identify stationary events as significant.
source: An alternative approach, the linear regression method, which samples from the posterior probability and uses linear regression to fit a line to the samples (Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Carr et al., 2011; Shin et al., 2019), detects only non-zero slopes as significant, and thus by definition cannot identify stationary events as significant.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section comparing the state space model to standard approaches with citations to Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Carr et al., 2011; Shin et al., 2019.

claim: The methods that rely on fitting a line for the entire SWR (Radon transform and linear regression) tend to estimate that replays proceed at faster speeds.
source: We found that the methods that rely on fitting a line for the entire SWR (the Radon transform and the linear regression), tend to estimate that the replays proceed at faster speeds (Figure 6A,C)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6A,C.

claim: The MAP method allows for more variable speeds and can capture both fast and slow speeds.
source: whereas the MAP method (Figure 6B), which only relies on picking the most probable position for a given time bin and allows for more variable speeds, meaning it can capture both fast and slow speeds.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The speeds from the MAP method are quite similar to the speeds estimated by the state space decoder.
source: In addition, the speeds from the MAP method (Figure 6B) are quite similar to the speeds estimated by the state space decoder (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by comparison of Figure 6B and Figure 6D.

claim: The state space decoder with 2 ms bins imposes much less smoothing than the linear methods and is closer to the MAP estimates with 20 ms bins.
source: Our state space decoder with 2 ms bins imposes much less smoothing than the linear methods and therefore is closer to the MAP estimates with 20 ms bins (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The state space decoder takes into account the uncertainty of each time bin.
source: but also takes into account the uncertainty of each time bin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The state space decoder is able to change direction more quickly than the 20 ms time bins.
source: and is able to change direction more quickly than the 20 ms time bins (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Methods that made more assumptions about the structure of replay (Radon and linear regression approaches) yield different conclusions about which events are potentially meaningful and how those events progress over time from methods that make fewer assumptions (MAP and state-space approaches).
source: These results indicate that the methods that made more assumptions about the structure of replay (Radon and linear regression approaches) yield different conclusions about which events are potentially meaningful and how those events progress over time from methods that make fewer assumptions (the MAP and state-space approaches).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the comparison of different methods.

claim: The state space model is robust and relatively insensitive to a range of plausible transition parameters between dynamics.
source: This model is robust: it is relatively insensitive to a range of plausible transition parameters between dynamics and instead strongly reflects the hippocampal place representation structure.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the model's properties.

claim: The state space model is interpretable with well-defined parameters that capture intuitive movement models.
source: We show that this model is interpretable: it has well-defined parameters that capture intuitive movement models and allows us to explain a large fraction of SWRs in terms of these dynamics—far more than have been previously associated with identifiable activity patterns.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the model's properties.

claim: The state space model is flexible and can be used with sorted or clusterless spikes, 1D or 2D positions.
source: This model is also flexible: it can be used with sorted or clusterless spikes, it can be used with 1D or 2D positions
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the model's properties.

claim: The state space model allows confident discovery of SWRs with spatial representations that move at a constant speed, vary in speed, have slower speeds, or are stationary.
source: and—because it uses a mixture of dynamics—it allows us to confidently discover not only SWRs with spatial representations that move at a constant speed, but also representations that vary in speed, have slower speeds, or that are stationary.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the model's capabilities.

claim: Slower moving representations constitute the majority of representations seen during SWRs.
source: In fact, these slower moving representations constitute the majority of representations seen during SWRs
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the findings.

claim: Hippocampal replay can recapitulate experience at both accelerated and closer to real-world speeds.
source: The prevalence of these events indicates that hippocampal replay can recapitulate experience at both accelerated and closer to real-world speeds.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the findings.

claim: Spatially coherent events most often expressed a dynamic that was consistent with slower speeds of less than 1 m/s (100 cm/s).
source: Importantly, the spatially coherent events most often expressed a dynamic that was consistent with slower speeds of less than 1 m/s (100 cm/s), a speed range that includes the speeds at which rats traverse their environment.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the findings.

claim: Classical replay events (continuous, extended trajectories through space) made up only about 19% of classified events.
source: while the 'classical' replay events—continuous, extended trajectories through space—made up only about 19% of classified events.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the findings.

claim: Events with slower dynamics tended to persist for approximately the same length of time as events with faster continuous dynamics (approximately 50-100 ms).
source: Events with slower dynamics tended to persist for approximately the same length of time as events with faster continuous dynamics (∼50–100 ms)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the findings.

claim: Events with slower dynamics most often represented the animal's current location, similar to continuous events identified in previous work.
source: Events with slower dynamics most often represented the animal's current location, similar to continuous events identified in previous work (Davidson et al., 2009; Karlsson and Frank, 2009)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Davidson et al., 2009; Karlsson and Frank, 2009.

claim: Slower events were also capable of representing locations far from the animal.
source: however, slower events were also capable of representing locations far from the animal.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the findings.

claim: Louie and Wilson, 2001 found that during REM sleep, the longer time scale population activity (on the order of seconds) is highly correlated with firing during times when the animal is running.
source: Interestingly, Louie and Wilson, 2001 found that during REM sleep, the longer time scale population activity (on the order of seconds) is highly correlated with firing during times when the animal is running, resembling the animal's experience.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Louie and Wilson, 2001.

claim: The findings challenge the long-held notion that hippocampal replay trajectories necessarily proceed at many times the speed of the animal.
source: These results challenge the long-held notion that hippocampal replay trajectories necessarily proceed at many times the speed of the animal (Nádasdy et al., 1999; Lee and Wilson, 2002; Davidson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Nádasdy et al., 1999; Lee and Wilson, 2002; Davidson et al., 2009.

claim: Replay events encompass a much richer variety of event speeds that could promote storage and updating of memories on different spatial and temporal scales.
source: Instead, replay events encompass a much richer variety of event speeds that could promote storage and updating of memories on different spatial and temporal scales, including slower moving representations that activate a spatially compact set of nearby locations and stationary representations of single locations.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: A previous paper (Farooq and Dragoi, 2019) reported that stationary representations were most prevalent in juvenile rats and decreased to 'chance' levels when the rats reached adulthood.
source: Interestingly, a previous paper (Farooq and Dragoi, 2019) reported that these stationary representations were most prevalent in juvenile rats and decreased to 'chance' levels when the rats reached adulthood.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Farooq and Dragoi, 2019.

claim: The findings strongly suggest that stationary representations do not disappear in adult rats but are a very common occurrence.
source: Our results strongly suggest that they do not disappear, but are a very common occurrence with adult rats.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the findings.

claim: Initial studies of replay focused on the question of whether the observed patterns of spiking seen during replay reflected structured content or 'random' spiking.
source: Initial studies of replay (Lee and Wilson, 2002; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Davidson et al., 2009; Karlsson and Frank, 2009) focused on the question of whether the observed patterns of spiking seen during replay reflected structured content or 'random' spiking as defined by a comparison to one or more shuffles.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Lee and Wilson, 2002; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Davidson et al., 2009; Karlsson and Frank, 2009.

claim: Initial studies of replay answered the question 'are replay events the result of random spiking?' with a clear 'no'.
source: These and subsequent studies answered the question 'are replay events the result of random spiking?' with a clear 'no'.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of previous findings.

claim: The significance criteria used in initial studies to show non-random structure has nothing to do with the presence of spatial structure or events that are potentially useful for memory processes.
source: These studies did not, however, establish that the significance criteria used to show non-random structure has anything to do with the presence of spatial structure or events that are potentially useful for memory processes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a critique of previous approaches.

claim: The method aims to identify structure within events and to capture their complex dynamics to determine what sort of information replay events could provide in service of memory functions.
source: Our method aims to identify structure within events and to capture their complex dynamics to determine what sort of information replay events could provide in service of memory functions.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a description of the method's goals.

claim: Most, but not all, events contain spiking that corresponds to a location or a trajectory through the animal's environment.
source: In so doing, we find that most, but not all, events contain spiking that corresponds to a location or a trajectory through the animal's environment.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the findings.

claim: 19% of SWRs contained continuous trajectories, but only 4% were continuous throughout the entire SWR.
source: Our results showed that 19% of SWRs contained continuous trajectories—meaning that portions of the SWR had spatially coherent trajectories that moved at high velocities—but only 4% were continuous throughout the entire SWR.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the findings.

claim: Previous studies found between 5% and 45% of SWRs were 'significant', meaning they were well fit by a line compared to various shuffled versions of the dataset.
source: This, prima facie, may seem at odds with previous results, which found between 5% and 45% of SWRs were 'significant', meaning that they were well fit by a line compared to various shuffled versions of the dataset.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a comparison to previous findings.

claim: Previous findings were based largely on a single linear fit to the data for each event, while the current model allows the trajectory to change speed during the SWR.
source: These previous findings were based largely on a single linear fits to the data for each event, while our model allows the trajectory to change speed during the SWR, which can lead to very different estimates of the speed of the event.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an explanation for differences with previous findings.

claim: Many events that had continuous dynamics also exhibited stationary-continuous mixture dynamics for some portion of the event.
source: Many of the events that had continuous dynamics, and would be classified as having high speed trajectories, also exhibited stationary-continuous mixture dynamics for some portion of the event(see for example Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by examples in Figure 2.

claim: The linear fit is highly sensitive to the definition of the start and end of the SWR event.
source: Further, because the linear fit includes the whole SWR event, it is highly sensitive to the definition of the start and end of the SWR event, an often arbitrary definition which varies across research groups.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a critique of previous approaches.

claim: The state space model makes an estimate for each time point and only depends on the previous and future time step, minimizing dependence on event boundaries.
source: In contrast, our model makes an estimate for each time point and only depends on the previous and future time step, which minimizes the dependence of the event on those boundaries and any possible 'noise' activity within the SWR.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an advantage of the current approach.

claim: The more permissive threshold for SWRs allows characterization of more SWRs than previous studies.
source: This, along with our more permissive threshold for SWRs, allows us to characterize more SWRs than previous studies, rather than exclude them from analysis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an explanation for differences with previous findings.

claim: Stella et al., 2019 reported that hippocampal replay trajectories followed Brownian-like diffusion dynamics.
source: Our results may also explain the seeming conflict between (Stella et al., 2019), who reported that hippocampal replay trajectories followed Brownian-like diffusion dynamics
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Stella et al., 2019.

claim: Pfeiffer and Foster, 2015 reported that a subset of replay trajectories contained systematic jumps in position.
source: and (Pfeiffer and Foster, 2015), who reported that a subset of replay trajectories contained systematic jumps in position.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Pfeiffer and Foster, 2015.

claim: Replay speeds are, on average, distributed log normally.
source: We found that while replay speeds are, on average, distributed log normally, a small subset of the replays include definitive 'jumps' from one position to another.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the findings.

claim: A small subset of replays include definitive 'jumps' from one position to another.
source: We found that while replay speeds are, on average, distributed log normally, a small subset of the replays include definitive 'jumps' from one position to another.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the findings.

claim: The model makes it possible to identify different dynamics within the same SWR.
source: Because our model makes it possible to identify different dynamics within the same SWR, we are able to identify both types of sequences.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an explanation for reconciling previous findings.

claim: The large set of events with slow dynamics would engage specific patterns of activity outside the hippocampus.
source: Thus, we would expect that the large set of events with slow dynamics would also engage specific patterns of activity outside the hippocampus
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis based on previous findings by Jadhav et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2017.

claim: Events with slow dynamics might allow animals to store or update the value of specific locations or short movement trajectories without generating full trajectories.
source: perhaps allowing animals to store or update the value of specific locations or short movement trajectories without having to generate full trajectories representing one of multiple ways to arrive at a location (Yu and Frank, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis with a citation to Yu and Frank, 2015.

claim: Events that contain multiple dynamics might help bind together experiences that occur in the same environment but at different places.
source: Events that contain multiple dynamics (e.g. two continuous representations separated by a brief fragmented representation) might also help bind together experiences that occur in the same environment but at different places
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis.

claim: Sustained spatially incoherent representations might represent coherent representations in other spatial environments or non-spatial experiences.
source: whereas sustained spatially incoherent representations might represent coherent representations in other spatial environments (Karlsson and Frank, 2009) or non-spatial experiences.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis with a citation to Karlsson and Frank, 2009.

claim: Downstream structures may be attuned to shifts in dynamics, with each period of coherent hippocampal dynamics driving its own set of responses elsewhere in the brain.
source: Alternatively, downstream structures may be are attuned to the shifts in dynamics, and that each period of coherent hippocampal dynamics drives its own set of responses elsewhere in the brain.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis.

claim: Recent results indicate that individual theta cycles can have different dynamics as well.
source: We further note that recent results from a study of activity patterns during movement indicates that individual theta cycles can have different dynamics as well (Wang et al., 2020)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Wang et al., 2020.

claim: The underlying sequences seen during replay and theta may overlap in their dynamics as well as their content.
source: suggesting that the underlying sequences seen during replay and theta may overlap in their dynamics as well as their content.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis based on Wang et al., 2020.

claim: Slow and fast dynamics may be supported by different subcircuits within the hippocampal formation.
source: Similarly, it is possible that slow and fast dynamics are supported by different subcircuits within the hippocampal formation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis.

claim: Yamamoto and Tonegawa, 2017 found that blocking medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) output to CA1 resulted in shorter (and therefore slower) replay trajectories.
source: Yamamoto and Tonegawa, 2017 found that blocking medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) output to CA1 resulted in shorter (and therefore slower) replay trajectories
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Yamamoto and Tonegawa, 2017.

claim: Oliva et al., 2018 showed that layer 2/3 MEC neurons increased their firing 50 ms before the start of longer duration SWRs (>100 ms).
source: and (Oliva et al., 2018) showed that layer 2/3 MEC neurons increased their firing 50 ms before the start of longer duration SWRs (>100 ms).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Oliva et al., 2018.

claim: Slower replays may be driven by CA3-CA1 interaction while faster trajectories are more externally driven by MEC-CA1.
source: This raises the possibility that these slower replays are driven by CA3-CA1 interaction while the faster trajectories are more externally driven by MEC-CA1
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis based on Yamamoto and Tonegawa, 2017 and Oliva et al., 2018.

claim: Different replay events could engage different circuits outside of the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex.
source: and that these different events could also engage different circuits outside of the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis.

claim: The method allows for moment-by-moment characterization of the neural dynamic.
source: Because our method allows for moment-by-moment characterization of the neural dynamic
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a description of the method's capabilities.

claim: Evaluating the start and end of each dynamic may prove a powerful way to identify periods of interest.
source: we suggest that evaluating the start and end of each dynamic may prove a powerful way identify periods of interest.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a suggestion for future research.

claim: A more permissive approach to event detection was critical for the identification of events that activate specific, immobility-associated locations in previous work.
source: This more permissive approach was also critical for the identification of events that activate specific, immobility-associated locations in previous work (Yu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Yu et al., 2017.

claim: There is no evidence that SWR and high population activity events constitute clearly distinct classes of events that can be identified with a single fixed threshold.
source: More broadly, there is no evidence that SWR and high population activity events constitute clearly distinct classes of events that can be identified with a single fixed threshold.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a critique of threshold-based approaches.

claim: The sizes of SWR and high population activity events are well described by a unimodal, long-tailed distribution.
source: Instead, the sizes of these events are well described by a unimodal, long-tailed distribution (Yu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Yu et al., 2017.

claim: High thresholds can exclude large numbers of real events and potentially lead to erroneous conclusions.
source: High thresholds can therefore exclude large numbers of real events and potentially lead to erroneous conclusions.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a critique of high threshold approaches.

claim: Clusterless decoding enabled taking advantage of information from neurons farther away from the tetrodes and not just those that could be cleanly separated.
source: Second, we used clusterless decoding, which enabled us to take advantage of information from neurons farther away from the tetrodes and not just those that could be cleanly and somewhat subjectively separated (Chen et al., 2012b; Kloosterman et al., 2014; Deng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Chen et al., 2012b; Kloosterman et al., 2014; Deng et al., 2016.

claim: More fully automated modern spike sorting algorithms in combination with better recording technology could reduce the differences in results when using sorted spikes or clusterless decoding.
source: We note that more fully automated modern spike sorting algorithms (such as MountainSort; Chung et al., 2017) in combination with better recording technology could reduce the differences in results when using sorted spikes or clusterless decoding
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Chung et al., 2017.

claim: An explicit and flexible model was built that allowed identification of not just one dynamic, but multiple dynamics consistent with different speeds of motion.
source: Third, we built an explicit and flexible model that allowed us to identify not just one dynamic, but multiple dynamics consistent with different speeds of motion.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a description of the method.

claim: The model avoided using large temporal bins and does not make assumptions about the linear progression of events.
source: Fourth, our model avoided using large temporal bins and does not make assumptions about the linear progression of events.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a description of the method.

claim: The model allows for movement in any direction allowed by geometry of the environment and accounts for the uncertainty of the data.
source: Instead, the model allows for movement in any direction allowed by geometry of the environment, and further, still accounts for the uncertainty of the data.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a description of the method.

claim: The model gives a moment-by-moment estimate of the position and dynamic, minimizing the effect of misidentifying the SWR start and end times.
source: Because the model gives a moment-by-moment estimate of the position and dynamic, this also minimizes the effect of misidentifying the SWR start and end times.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an advantage of the method.

claim: Combined with acausal estimation of latent position, the approach allows identification of the specific timing of transitions in dynamics at a fine timescale.
source: Combined with an acausal estimation of latent position, this approach allows us to identify the specific timing of transitions in dynamics at a fine timescale.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an advantage of the method.

claim: The approach could be used to decode activity during movement, where place-specific activity would express combinations of stationary and continuous dynamics reflecting different speeds of representational movement during each theta cycle.
source: In addition to our SWR-based analyses, this approach could also be used to decode activity during movement, where we might expect that place-specific activity would express combinations of stationary and continuous dynamics reflecting different speeds of representational movement during each cycle of the theta rhythm.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a suggestion for future applications.

claim: The approach could be used to investigate sequence dynamics before experience.
source: Similarly, because our approach uses the same encoder-decoder approach as the standard decoder, it can be used to investigate sequence dynamics before experience (Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a suggestion for future applications with a citation to Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2013.

claim: The model can be viewed as an extension to the multiple temporal models approach of Johnson et al., 2008.
source: Our model can be viewed as an extension to the multiple temporal models approach of Johnson et al., 2008, which used model selection to determine the model with the most appropriate trajectory speed.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Johnson et al., 2008.

claim: The model goes beyond the Johnson model by explicitly permitting a mixture between movement speeds, working for arbitrary track geometries, and using clusterless decoding.
source: Our model goes beyond the Johnson model in that it explicitly permits a mixture between the movement speeds, can work for arbitrary track geometries, and uses clusterless decoding.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a comparison to Johnson et al., 2008.

claim: The model represents a middle ground between Hidden Markov-style models and the standard decoder.
source: Our model also represents a middle ground between Hidden Markov-style models (Chen et al., 2012a; Chen et al., 2016; Linderman et al., 2016; Maboudi et al., 2018), which seek to be environment-agnostic detectors of sequential patterns, and the standard decoder, which typically use arbitrarily chosen bin sizes and restrictive assumptions about the nature of the trajectories.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Chen et al., 2012a; Chen et al., 2016; Linderman et al., 2016; Maboudi et al., 2018.

claim: The approach allows for a variety of dynamics while still yielding spatially interpretable results and makes it possible to use bin sizes of any size.
source: In particular, our approach allows for a variety of dynamics while still yielding spatially interpretable results and makes it possible to use bin sizes of any size (here 2 ms).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an advantage of the method.

claim: Code and algorithms for decoding hippocampal replay have not typically been made accessible or easy to use.
source: Code and algorithms for decoding hippocampal replay have not typically been made accessible or easy to use.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a critique of the field.

claim: Lack of accessible code can lead to severe variation or errors in code and parameters, limits reproducibility of results, and slows down scientific progress.
source: This is problematic because it can lead to severe variation or errors in code and parameters, limits reproducibility of results, and slows down scientific progress.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a critique of the field.

claim: Code for the model has been made publicly available as a python package.
source: Accordingly, we have made code for this model publicly available as a python package at the following URL https://github.com/Eden-Kramer-Lab/replay_trajectory_classification (Denovellis, 2021a; copy archived at swh:1:rev:83d84170ae0bdeef65cd123fa83448fcca9cb986).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a URL and citation to Denovellis, 2021a.

claim: The code is easily installable using the pip or conda package installer and contains tutorial Jupyter notebooks.
source: It is easily installable using the pip or conda package installer and contains tutorial Jupyter notebooks in order to facilitate reuse.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a description of the code availability.

claim: State-space models can enable a richer set of analyses of events that take advantage of all of the available data.
source: State-space models like the one we use here can enable a richer set of analyses of events that take advantage of all of the available data.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion about the method.

claim: These approaches can be applied not just to SWRs but to all times, providing a moment-by-moment estimate of the nature of the spatial representation in the hippocampus.
source: These approaches can be applied not just to SWRs but to all times, providing a moment-by-moment estimate of the nature of the spatial representation in the hippocampus, including important information about the spatial coherence of that representation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a suggestion for future applications.

claim: The model can be extended to incorporate other previously experienced environments by training place field models on those environments.
source: The model can be extended to incorporate other previously experienced environments by training place field models on those environments and including the appropriate movement transition matrices for those environments.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a suggestion for future extensions.

claim: The model can be extended to account for task conditions and forward/reverse sequences.
source: It can also be extended to account for task conditions (such as the inbound and outbound conditions in our spatial alternation task) and forward/reverse sequences as in Deng et al., 2016.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a suggestion for future extensions with a citation to Deng et al., 2016.

claim: Models can be built to estimate any covariate, including movement direction.
source: Finally, models can be built to estimate any covariate, including movement direction (Kay et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a suggestion for future extensions with a citation to Kay et al., 2020.

claim: The approach has the potential to provide a much richer understanding of neural representations throughout the brain.
source: We therefore suggest that this approach has the potential to provide a much richer understanding of neural representations throughout the brain.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion about the broader implications of the method.
